cues.captionText: Your AI agent handled the same number of tasks this month as
last month. But the bill climbed from six hundred dollars to twenty-four
hundred. Nothing obvious changed in the dashboard. So what happened?
Here is the explanation. A workflow can repeat tool calls,
retry failed steps, or ask another model for help.
If nobody measures the number of paid actions required for an accepted
result, the budget can rise even while the workload stays flat.
I will show the math, then give you three controls to put
in place before an agent touches your business: a spending limit,
an authority limit, and an evidence trail. The example is fictional,
with clear assumptions, so you can replace the numbers with your own.
Start with two hundred tasks per day, for thirty days.
That is six thousand tasks. Assume each paid model or tool call
costs two cents. The exact price is hypothetical, not a vendor quote.
In month one, each task uses five paid calls.
Six thousand times five times two cents equals six hundred dollars.
In month two, each task uses twenty paid calls.
Six thousand times twenty times two cents equals twenty-four hundred dollars.
The task count did not change.
The paid calls per task rose fourfold.
This calculation isolates call charges. It excludes hosting, data storage,
external software, integration, human review, and the cost of fixing
mistakes. If those costs rise too,
the total bill can be higher.
The metric to watch is not only cost per call.
Watch paid calls per attempted task, cost per accepted result,
and the percentage of tasks that fail or need human repair.
Those three numbers expose whether your workflow is doing useful work or
paying to repeat itself.
There is a reason to take these controls seriously. On October twenty-second,
Cognizant published a survey of two hundred and fifty senior FinOps leaders
at large organizations in the United States, United Kingdom and India.
Seventy-two percent of the surveyed organizations had exceeded their AI budgets in
the preceding twelve months. The survey was vendor-sponsored and does not establish
the rate for every business.
The useful takeaway is narrower: leaders need cost visibility tied to work
performed, not a dashboard showing token totals without a business outcome.
On October twenty-seventh, IBM announced new AI-agent identity
and control capabilities. Its announcement separates currently available
evaluation functions from discovery and containment functions described
as technology previews. Vendor announcements are not independent
evidence of customer savings.
These developments point toward the same operating discipline.
Count what an agent spends. Define what it is allowed to do.
Preserve proof of the result.
The first control is a budget limit at three levels.
At the individual call level, set a maximum cost and maximum response
size where your provider supports them. At the task level,
limit the number of paid calls and retries. At the daily level,
stop the workflow when its approved spending allocation is reached.
Suppose a task is allowed eight paid calls.
If call nine becomes necessary, do not let the agent silently keep
going. Pause the task, log the reason, and route it to a
person or an approved fallback.
Here is the distinction between an alert and a control.
An email saying you spent too much is an alert.
A budget enforcement point that blocks the next charge is a control.
You also need a failure rule. When a tool times out,
the agent should not retry forever. Set a retry count,
a backoff interval, and an escalation path. When the task fails,
record the failure. Do not label it as a completed result.
For a small pilot, a simple ledger and a wrapper around
paid tool calls are enough to test this design.
Production enforcement requires reliable accounting and provider-specific limits.
The second control is an authority limit. A useful agent needs enough
access to complete a defined job,
but not unlimited access to the company.
Take a purchasing assistant. It might read an approved supplier
catalogue and prepare a comparison. That does not mean it
should place orders, alter banking details,
or approve invoices without separate authorization.
Give each agent a named owner, a specific job,
and only the permissions required for that job.
Use short-lived credentials where supported. Keep payment, deletion, external publication,
and other irreversible actions behind an explicit approval step.
Make sure a responsible operator can revoke access.
Think of the workflow as a series of gates.
Read approved information. Propose a decision. Validate the proposal.
Obtain approval for a sensitive action. Execute. Verify the result.
A prompt that says, 'Do not spend money,' is not a financial
control. The actual tool must enforce the restriction. A written policy helps,
but a blocked transaction is stronger evidence.
The third control is an evidence trail. For each run,
record a task identifier, its owner, the input category,
every tool call, cost, retry, exception, human approval, and final outcome.
Do not store unnecessary personal information in the log.
Protect sensitive records and define a retention period.
Then create an acceptance test. If the agent extracts invoice data,
compare the fields against a checked reference. If it produces a supplier
shortlist, check the requirements and source dates. If it drafts an email,
a reviewer approves before sending.
Now calculate the metric that matters: total operating cost divided by
accepted outputs. Include the human review and rework costs where you have reliable data.
Here is a second fictional example. An agent completes one hundred
tasks, but only eighty pass quality checks.
The model and tool charges are forty dollars.
Human review and corrections cost another sixty dollars.
The combined one hundred dollars divided by eighty accepted outputs equals
one dollar and twenty-five cents per accepted result.
If you only report forty cents per attempted task,
you hide the cost of failed results and human repair.
That makes the agent look cheaper than the workflow really is.
Before scaling an agent, run a controlled pilot with a written scorecard.
Pick one workflow with clear inputs and a measurable outcome.
Record the manual baseline: cost, elapsed time, error rate, and human effort.
Then run the agent on a comparable task set.
Measure six items. One: accepted output rate. Two:
cost per accepted output, including review. Three:
median and slow-end completion time. Four:
tool calls and retries per task. Five:
unauthorized-action attempts and blocked actions. Six:
operator time spent on exceptions.
Set pass and stop conditions before the pilot. For example,
stop automatically if a task exceeds eight paid calls,
if an approval is missing, or if a required field fails validation.
Those numbers are illustrative and should be tuned to the actual workflow.
Do not calculate return on investment from time saved unless the time
has a defensible value. Released staff capacity is not the same thing
as cash savings. Show both separately.
When the pilot passes, increase volume in stages.
Check whether cost per accepted output stays stable as volume grows.
If quality drops or exception handling rises, do not scale on the
strength of a headline productivity percentage.
Here is the decision framework in one sentence.
Do not approve an AI agent because it answers quickly.
Approve it when its cost, authority and accepted outcomes are measurable.
Before your next rollout, ask three questions.
What stops spending when the workflow goes wrong?
What prevents an unauthorized action? And what evidence proves the task was completed correctly?
If the answers are unclear, run a smaller pilot and fix the
controls before giving the agent more responsibility.
